fixes.explanation: That's the exact phrase. Job says, "I have heard many things like these; miserable comforters are you all." (Job 16:2) Eliphaz, one of his three friends (Job 2:11), had just finished his speech (Job 15). I bet Job was hoping for a hug and got a lecture instead.

Nope, Job isn't handing out compliments here. He says, "miserable comforters are you all." (Job 16:2) His three friends came to sympathize with him and comfort him (Job 2:11), and Job calls them miserable comforters. Think of a friend who brings you a cookie box with nothing in it.

Yes, he says it. Job tells his friends, "I could also speak like you if you were in my place; I could heap up words against you and shake my head at you." (Job 16:4) He knows how to talk like that. The next verse says what he'd do instead.

Job doesn't say he'd grill them. He says, "But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief." (Job 16:5) Encouragement and relief are the goal. Nobody ever felt better after a coworker fired off a list of questions on a hard day.
Right. Job says, "Surely He has now exhausted me; You have devastated all my family." (Job 16:7) That's the weight he's carrying. I think this one hurts.
Footstool isn't the word Job uses in this verse. He says, "He has set me up as His target…" (Job 16:12) The next verse brings in archers (Job 16:13), so target fits the picture. It's target, friend.
Silent isn't Job's word. He says, "…yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure." (Job 16:17) The blank wants pure, friend.

Right, it's false. Job says, "O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest." (Job 16:18) He asks for the opposite: no covering of his blood, and no resting for his cry for help.
The city gate isn't where Job points. He says, "Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high." (Job 16:19) His witness is in heaven, friend.

That's right. Job says, "Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!" (Job 16:21) He wishes a man could plead with God the way he would plead with his neighbor. It's a wish, and he says it out loud.

This one is true, friend. Job says, "Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!" (Job 16:21) Look at the comparison: pleading with God, the way a man pleads with his neighbor. That's the wish, right there in the verse.
Not a move, friend. Job says, "For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return." (Job 16:22) He's talking about the end of his life. This part is heavy, so we let it be heavy.

Mourners isn't the word. Job says, "Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must gaze at their rebellion." (Job 17:2) Mockers are what he sees. I think he'd want comfort, and that makes this view even harder.
Other way around, friend. Job says, "You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore You will not exalt them." (Job 17:4) Exalted is exactly what he says they will not be.
Tent doesn't fit this verse. Job says, "…a man in whose face they spit." (Job 17:6) The spitting is in his face. Face is the word that fills the blank.
Looking away isn't what Job says. He says, "The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred against the godless." (Job 17:8) Appalled is the word he uses for the upright.
Job says the opposite. He tells them, "For I will not find a wise man among you." (Job 17:10) A wise man is exactly what he says he won't find.
Job doesn't ask where his friends are. He asks, "…where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?" (Job 17:15) His question is about hope.
This one is true, friend. Job ends with, "Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?" (Job 17:16) He closes on a question. The story isn't over, though.
